hypotheses.justification: `hf_int` follows from `hf`, so it can be dropped. Because `f` is continuous, it is `AEStronglyMeasurable`, so the only thing to check is that `∫⁻ ‖f‖ₑ` is finite. Take the compact cube K = `Set.Icc 0 1`, the same `hK` that the proof of `mFourierCoeff_eq_piFourierIntegral` already builds. That proof also has `hFD`, which says that `pi univ (fun _ => Ico 0 1)` is an additive fundamental domain for the ℤ-lattice. Mathlib's `IsAddFundamentalDomain.lintegral_eq_tsum''` (the additive form of `lintegral_eq_tsum''` in MeasureTheory/Group/FundamentalDomain.lean) then gives `∫⁻ ‖f‖ₑ = ∑' g, ∫⁻ x in cube, ‖f (g +ᵥ x)‖ₑ`. Each summand is at most `‖(f.comp (addRight (intVec n))).restrict K‖ * vol(cube) = ‖…restrict K‖`, using `norm_coe_le_norm` and the fact that the cube has volume 1, exactly as in the existing estimate `hG_sum_int`. The right-hand side is summable by `hf K`, so the integral is finite and `f` is integrable. The degenerate case `d` empty is harmless: `d → ℝ` is then a single point and `volume` is a probability measure. So `mFourierCoeff_eq_piFourierIntegral` can derive `hef_int` from `hf`, and the rest of the proof is unchanged. This matches Mathlib's one-dimensional `Real.tsum_eq_tsum_fourier`, which takes only `h_norm` (the same as `hf`) and `h_sum`, with no integrability hypothesis.
